title: OpenID Connect & SSO
summary: The identity layer OIDC adds on top of OAuth's authorization plumbing, and how single sign-on lets one login serve many applications. Closes this group by finally making 'Continue with Google' an actual login, not just delegated access.

slides.markdown:
[OAuth 2.0](oauth2) closed on a deliberate gap: it's authorization, not authentication — it proves a token grants some access, and says nothing about who the user actually is. **OpenID Connect (OIDC)** is the standard that fills that gap, layering an identity assertion on top of OAuth's exact same flow.

This is the topic that finally makes "Continue with Google" an actual login rather than just delegated data access, and it's also where **single sign-on (SSO)** — one login serving many applications — gets its modern mechanism. This closes the Authentication & Authorization group: everything from [Authentication Fundamentals](authn-fundamentals) through OAuth converges here into the standard that powers most real-world "login with X" buttons.

slides.sectionTitle: OAuth2 is authorization, not authentication — why OIDC exists
slides.markdown:
Before OIDC, developers building "login with Google" hacked around OAuth's identity gap: they'd run the OAuth flow to get an access token, then call an API endpoint with that token and infer "since this token works and returns *some* user's profile, that must be who's logged in." This is fragile — an access token proves the bearer has some scoped access, not that a specific human authenticated *right now*, and a token obtained for one purpose could be misused to spoof a login if the inference wasn't done carefully.

OIDC formalizes what those hacks were reaching for: it defines a standard way for the Authorization Server to explicitly assert **"this specific user authenticated, just now, and here's cryptographic proof."** It's built as a thin, standardized identity layer on top of OAuth's existing flow — same redirect dance, same code exchange — rather than a competing protocol, which is exactly why so many providers that already spoke OAuth added OIDC support without rearchitecting anything.

OIDC's core addition is a second token issued alongside the OAuth access token: the **ID token**, and the two have genuinely different purposes despite both being JWTs in practice.

- **Access token** — proves the bearer has permission to call the **Resource Server** (Google's Calendar API, for instance). It's opaque by design in the OAuth spec — the Client isn't supposed to inspect its contents, only present it.
- **ID token** — a JWT specifically meant to be **read by the Client**, containing claims about the authentication event itself: `sub` (the user's stable ID), `iss` (which Authorization Server issued it), `aud` (which Client it's meant for), `exp`, and `iat` (when the authentication happened).

The audience distinction is the practical rule to remember: the access token is a bearer credential you *use*; the ID token is a signed identity claim you *read* to establish who just logged in. Using an access token to determine identity — the pre-OIDC hack — conflates these two genuinely different jobs.

The ID token is deliberately kept small — it's meant to be verified quickly and often re-sent — so it carries only the core authentication claims. For richer profile data, OIDC defines a standard **`/userinfo`** endpoint: the Client calls it with the access token, and gets back additional standard claims (`name`, `email`, `email_verified`, `picture`, and more) in a consistent shape across any OIDC-compliant provider.

That standardization is the underrated part: because every OIDC provider exposes the same claim names for the same concepts, a Client written to consume "login with any OIDC provider" doesn't need custom parsing logic per provider the way ad hoc "login with X" integrations historically did — swapping from "Login with Google" to "Login with Okta" is largely a configuration change, not a rewrite, as long as both speak OIDC.

The `email_verified` claim specifically is worth knowing by name: it's the difference between "this provider has an email on file for this user" and "this provider has actually confirmed the user controls that email address" — a distinction that matters directly for account-linking security, covered next.

slides.sectionTitle: Single sign-on: one login, many applications
slides.markdown:
**Single sign-on (SSO)** is the user-facing payoff of standardizing identity this way: authenticate once with a central Identity Provider (IdP), and every application that trusts that IdP recognizes you as logged in, without a separate username and password per app.

Mechanically, this is OIDC's flow repeated per application, but with a UX shortcut: if you've already authenticated with the IdP recently (it maintains its own session with you, separate from any individual app's session), the IdP can skip re-prompting for credentials and immediately issue a fresh ID token for the *next* app you visit — you see a near-instant redirect rather than another login form. Log out of the IdP centrally, and (with the right implementation) every connected app's session can be invalidated too, rather than needing a separate logout per app.

This is exactly why enterprises standardize on one IdP (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace) rather than letting every internal tool run its own login: one place to enforce MFA, one place to revoke an offboarded employee's access across every connected system at once, instead of chasing down credentials app by app.

Before OIDC, enterprise SSO ran almost entirely on **SAML** (Security Assertion Markup Language), and it's still the standard you'll meet in large, established enterprise environments even though OIDC has largely won for new consumer-facing and modern web integrations.

The core difference is shape and era: SAML uses **XML** assertions exchanged via browser redirects and form posts, designed in the early 2000s primarily for enterprise, browser-based SSO into internal web applications. OIDC uses **JSON/JWT** over REST-style redirects, designed for the modern web including mobile apps and single-page apps that SAML's XML/form-post model handles awkwardly.

You'll encounter SAML specifically when integrating with established enterprise identity providers (many large companies' internal IdPs still speak SAML alongside or instead of OIDC) — knowing the name and the era it comes from is enough breadth for most engineering contexts; deep SAML implementation detail is a specialist skill, not a general expectation.

slides.sectionTitle: An OIDC login handing back both tokens
slides.markdown:
![OIDC sequence diagram showing the same OAuth Authorization Code flow with one added openid scope and both an ID token and access token returned](assets/oidc-sequence.svg)

The diagram's point is how little OIDC actually changes mechanically: it's the identical Authorization Code flow from the OAuth topic, with one additional requested scope (`openid`) and one additional token in the response. The entire identity layer rides on OAuth's existing plumbing rather than replacing any of it.

assets.alt: OIDC sequence diagram showing the same OAuth Authorization Code flow with one added openid scope and both an ID token and access token returned

slides.sectionTitle: OIDC vs SAML: modern web vs enterprise identity
slides.markdown:
| | OIDC | SAML |
|---|---|---|
| **Format** | JSON / JWT | XML |
| **Era / origin** | Modern web, built on OAuth 2.0 | Early 2000s enterprise SSO |
| **Mobile / SPA support** | Native fit — same OAuth flow, PKCE-compatible | Awkward — designed around full-page browser redirects and form posts |
| **Where you'll meet it** | Consumer "login with X," modern SaaS integrations | Established enterprise IdPs, legacy internal tooling |
| **Underlying transport** | REST-style redirects | Browser redirects + HTML form posts carrying XML |

The practical reality for most engineers: greenfield work defaults to OIDC, but integrating with an existing large enterprise's identity infrastructure means SAML support is often non-negotiable, since that's genuinely what their IdP speaks — knowing both exist and why is more valuable than being deeply fluent in SAML's XML schema specifically.

slides.sectionTitle: Using an OAuth2 access token to "authenticate" a user
slides.markdown:
The exact mistake OIDC was created to close, and one that still shows up in codebases that predate OIDC's widespread adoption or were built by developers unaware of the distinction: treating "I successfully called an API with this access token" as proof of who the user is.

Why it's unsound even when it happens to work: an OAuth access token's job is authorizing calls to a Resource Server, not asserting identity — nothing in the OAuth spec guarantees the token you're holding corresponds to a specific, freshly-authenticated human, and depending on scope and provider behavior, tokens can sometimes be used in ways that don't map cleanly to "this exact user is currently present." Building login logic on top of that inference means your authentication security depends on assumptions about a token's behavior that OAuth never actually promised.

The fix is using OIDC properly: request the `openid` scope, receive a genuine **ID token**, and verify its signature plus its `aud` (audience) and `exp` claims before trusting it — that's a token whose entire, documented purpose is asserting exactly the thing you want to know. If a login integration is calling a random authenticated API endpoint and inferring identity from a successful response, that's the specific smell to flag in review.

This closes Authentication & Authorization. Across all seven topics, one distinction kept recurring in different forms: **who you are versus what you're allowed to do**, and **something proven once versus something re-verified on every request**. Sessions and JWT are two different answers to carrying proof of identity forward; RBAC/ABAC/ACLs are different answers to modeling what that identity can do; OAuth and OIDC are the standardized way to do both of those things *across* organizational boundaries instead of within a single system.

Together with Application Security's input-handling categories from the previous group, that's the OWASP Top 10 mapped end to end — the two groups' opening topics, [OWASP Top 10 Overview](owasp-top-10) and [Authentication Fundamentals](authn-fundamentals), were the map; everything since has been the mechanism underneath it.
